claims.claim: Injection moulding prepares thermoplastic melt, fills a closed mould, cools/solidifies sufficiently and ejects a part in a repeatable cycle.
claims.exclusions: Specialised variants may add or alter stages.
claims.basis: Both standards define injection-moulding practice and controlled preparation of thermoplastic specimens.

claims.claim: A production process must satisfy part requirements while remaining within material, machine, mould and safety limits.
claims.exclusions: Does not define product acceptance or equipment limits.
claims.basis: Standards support material-specific conditions and machinery safety boundaries; product-specific quality requirements remain external.

claims.claim: Moulding conditions cannot be treated as transferable universal constants across materials and production systems.
claims.exclusions: A controlling grade or machine document may define narrow values for its scope.
claims.basis: Both explicitly require material-specific moulding conditions or recognize that reproducible conditions vary by material.

claims.section: How to think like a process engineer
claims.claim: Process changes should be tied to measured outcomes and controlled comparisons rather than copied settings.
claims.exclusions: Does not mandate one experimental design.
claims.basis: Consistent process descriptions and reporting support controlled comparison, but the broader experimental method needs dedicated statistics evidence before verification.

claims.claim: Reciprocating-screw recovery meters and plasticises material for the next shot while adding thermal and mechanical history.
claims.exclusions: Exact plasticising mechanism and controls are machine/material specific.
claims.basis: Manufacturer guides describe screw plasticising and thermal/residence considerations; a machine-manufacturer source is still preferred.

claims.claim: During filling, melt traverses nozzle, feed system, gate and cavity, with upstream machine pressure including losses before the cavity.
claims.exclusions: Does not quantify losses.
claims.basis: Standards support process-stage terminology, but direct cavity-versus-machine pressure interpretation requires stronger sensor/process literature.

claims.claim: Fill-to-pack transfer changes the process control objective and post-fill pressure influence depends on the actual material/mould system.
claims.exclusions: No universal transfer percentage or packing value.
claims.basis: Stage descriptions are supported; dedicated switchover evidence is registered elsewhere in the Book audit.

claims.claim: Cooling and ejection readiness depend on material, geometry and mould thermal condition rather than elapsed time alone.
claims.exclusions: No universal cooling or ejection time.
claims.basis: Manufacturer guidance supports material/geometry-sensitive cooling and shrinkage; broad ejection wording needs mould-design literature for full support.

claims.section: Treat the cycle as an interacting system
claims.claim: Cycle stages are physically coupled, so thermal and pressure history in one stage can affect later behaviour.
claims.exclusions: Does not quantify coupling.
claims.basis: Material processing guidance and standardized process descriptions support interaction, but this remains an engineering synthesis rather than one controlling clause.

claims.claim: A reciprocating-screw injection unit commonly includes feed, heated barrel, screw, non-return function and nozzle to prepare and deliver melt.
claims.exclusions: Component design and terminology vary.
claims.basis: Manufacturer material guides describe compatible injection-unit components, but an injection-machine manufacturer manual should anchor final machine anatomy.

claims.claim: The clamping unit closes/supports the mould, provides clamping action, opens it and supports ejection-related operation.
claims.exclusions: Architecture differs among toggle, two-platen, hydraulic, electric and hybrid machines.
claims.basis: ISO scope covers clamping-area hazards but public abstract is insufficient for detailed architecture; machine-manufacturer documentation is required.

claims.claim: Machine controllers coordinate process commands and safety-related interfaces but a process display is not a complete map of hazardous energy.
claims.applicability: Injection moulding machines within ISO 20430 scope.
claims.exclusions: Exact controls and energy sources are machine-specific.
claims.basis: Safety standard supports significant hazards and safe-use information; detailed energy-system claims need machine manuals.

claims.claim: Setup, guarding, isolation, ratings and permitted operation must follow the specific machine manufacturer's instructions and site procedures.
claims.exclusions: Generic Book content cannot supersede controlling documentation.
claims.basis: Machinery safety framework requires safe-use information and equipment-specific controls; exact procedures remain external.

claims.section: The mould creates the part-forming space
claims.claim: Core/cavity surfaces define moulded geometry while the mould also provides feed, heat-transfer, separation and release functions.
claims.exclusions: Specific tool architectures vary.
claims.basis: ISO provides component terminology; detailed functional claims need a tooling engineering source before full verification.

claims.claim: Sprue/runner/gate or hot-runner elements convey melt and gate/feed geometry can affect filling and post-fill response.
claims.applicability: Moulds with conventional or heated feed systems.
claims.exclusions: No dimensional design rule asserted.
claims.basis: Terminology and manufacturer processing guidance support the concept; exact gate effects are mould/material specific.

claims.claim: Injection moulds use guidance/support and ejection components whose arrangement must be identified from the actual tool.
claims.exclusions: Not all tools use the same mechanisms.
claims.basis: ISO terminology standard documents mould components and equivalent terms without implying one universal construction.

claims.claim: A mould-temperature controller setpoint alone does not prove uniform cavity-surface temperature because circuit layout and heat load matter.
claims.exclusions: Magnitude depends on tool and coolant system.
claims.basis: Manufacturer guide supports mould-temperature control importance; dedicated heat-transfer evidence is needed for full generalization.

claims.claim: Amorphous and semi-crystalline thermoplastics differ in solidification and can differ in shrinkage, thermal response and dimensional behaviour.
claims.exclusions: Family classification does not determine exact grade behaviour.
claims.basis: Independent manufacturer families illustrate semi-crystalline PBT and amorphous high-performance thermoplastics with materially different processing/shrinkage behaviour.

claims.section: Do not turn the categories into absolutes
claims.claim: Additives, reinforcement and formulation can materially alter flow, crystallisation, shrinkage and warpage within a polymer family.
claims.exclusions: Effects and magnitude are formulation-specific.
claims.basis: Manufacturer and peer-reviewed evidence show formulation and fibre orientation materially influence processing and dimensional behaviour.

claims.section: Flow resistance is not a single material number
claims.claim: Apparent polymer-melt viscosity depends on material and conditions such as temperature and shear rate, so an unscoped viscosity value is incomplete.
claims.exclusions: Quantitative curves require material-specific rheology data.
claims.basis: Manufacturer processing guides reflect temperature/rate sensitivity, but a dedicated rheology reference should anchor the fundamental wording.

claims.section: Pressure is evidence about the whole flow path
claims.claim: A change in machine injection pressure can arise from combined melt and flow-path effects and does not uniquely identify one cause.
claims.exclusions: Specific sensor locations can narrow interpretation.
claims.basis: Needs dedicated pressure-loss/cavity-pressure evidence before this broad diagnostic statement is verified.

claims.section: Families are useful maps, not recipes
claims.claim: Polymer-family labels can orient engineering expectations but do not define a universal production process window.
claims.exclusions: Exact grade documentation controls.
claims.basis: ASTM defers to material-specific conditions and manufacturer families publish materially different processing requirements.

claims.section: The grade is the actionable identity
claims.claim: Grades within one polymer family can differ through molecular architecture and additives, so production decisions should resolve the exact commercial grade and current supplier information.
claims.exclusions: Does not imply supplier data alone proves process capability.
claims.basis: ASTM places material-specific guidance above generic practice and grade data sheets provide distinct processing requirements.

claims.claim: Fibres and other modifiers can change stiffness, flow, shrinkage, anisotropy, appearance and thermal behaviour.
claims.exclusions: Magnitude and direction depend on formulation.
claims.basis: Manufacturer and micro-CT research evidence support reinforcement-dependent anisotropy and dimensional/property changes.

claims.section: Do not transfer settings between modified grades by name alone
claims.claim: Processing settings should not be assumed interchangeable between unfilled, reinforced, flame-retarded or otherwise modified grades.
claims.exclusions: Transfer may be possible only when supplier evidence establishes equivalence.
claims.basis: Material-specific conditions and manufacturer grade differentiation directly support this restriction.

claims.claim: During screw recovery, material is conveyed and melted/mixed while the screw retracts to meter the next shot.
claims.exclusions: Heating/mechanical contributions vary by machine and material.
claims.basis: Material manufacturer guidance discusses screw plasticising requirements; a machine-manufacturer reference is still needed for generic machine operation.

claims.section: The non-return valve matters during injection
claims.claim: The non-return function limits reverse melt flow during injection; wear or poor sealing can contribute to shot inconsistency but is not proven by cushion/weight variation alone.
claims.exclusions: Valve design and diagnostic method are machine-specific.
claims.basis: Grade guide discusses check-ring/non-return arrangements; causal diagnostics need machine-manufacturer evidence.

claims.claim: Material suppliers may specify screw/nozzle/configuration requirements that override generic Book descriptions.
claims.exclusions: Machine ratings and approvals also control.
claims.basis: Both manufacturer sources provide material-scoped equipment recommendations.

claims.claim: Screw-position and cushion values are useful process signals but their exact meaning depends on machine position conventions and control architecture.
claims.exclusions: No universal cushion target.
claims.basis: Needs machine-manufacturer documentation defining position/cushion semantics and repeatability.

claims.claim: Machine suitability cannot be established from one universal shot-utilisation percentage because residence, plasticising capacity, pressure/rate, metering and clamp requirements interact.
claims.exclusions: Manufacturer-specific suitability limits may be valid in their scope.
claims.basis: Material guidance shows residence and equipment dependencies; final wording needs injection-machine manufacturer guidance.

claims.section: Velocity command and pressure demand are different quantities
claims.claim: During velocity-controlled filling the machine commands motion while pressure develops to overcome resistance up to applicable limits.
claims.exclusions: Control loop and pressure-limit behavior are controller-specific.
claims.basis: Process parameter distinction is consistent with standard reporting, but controller behavior needs machine-manufacturer evidence.

claims.section: A process should distinguish control from limits
claims.claim: Repeated contact with a pressure limit can prevent commanded velocity from being achieved and should not be treated as equivalent to intentional pressure-controlled filling.
claims.applicability: Controllers with pressure limiting during velocity control.
claims.exclusions: Exact response depends on controller design.
claims.basis: Requires current machine/controller documentation before verification.

claims.claim: Fill-to-pack transfer changes the process control objective and transfer criteria are not portable universal values across moulds.
claims.applicability: Injection processes with a fill-to-pack transition.
claims.exclusions: Exact switchover method is machine/process specific.
claims.basis: Stage concepts are supported; stronger switchover-specific research is registered in the high-risk resolution ledger.

summary.rule: No chapter is verified from this audit; hold blocks promotion and qualified wording must preserve scope/exclusions.
